title: Roman Governors, Procurators and Prefects
lead: Rome ruled its provinces through senators (legates and proconsuls) and Roman Knights (procurators and prefects). The Gospels and Acts name several: Pontius Pilate, Felix, Festus and Gallio.

sections.h: How the system looked in AD 69
sections.b: Wikipedia says a procurator was an official, always an equestrian, in charge of a province's finance, that smaller imperial provinces could be governed by a procurator, that Egypt was run by a prefect, and that the Pilate Stone shows Pilate's title was prefect. Tacitus shows the system in Book 1: Knights govern Egypt, with Tiberius Alexander then in charge (1:11); other provinces are held by procurators (1:11); legates command the armies (1:8-9); and procurators kill (1:7) and are killed (1:58).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:7; Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Histories of Tacitus 1:58

sections.b: Pontius Pilate governed Judea in Tiberius's fifteenth year (Luke 3:1). Felix is "the governor" at Caesarea (Acts 23:24), Festus comes after him (Acts 25:11-12), and Gallio is proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12). Josephus says Claudius made Judea a province after Agrippa's death and sent Cuspius Fadus as procurator, then Tiberius Alexander (Jewish War 2.11.6; Antiquities 20.5.2).
